guide.example: Someone earning {{base}} a month plus {{seniorityPay}} of diuturnidades, with a contract that began on {{start}} and ended on {{end}}, has {{seniority}} years of seniority. The daily amount is {{daily}}. The contract began between 1 November 2011 and 30 September 2013, so {{twentyYears}} years up to 30 September 2013 count 20 days ({{twentyAmount}}), {{eighteenYears}} years complete the first three years at 18 days ({{eighteenAmount}}), {{twelveYears}} years up to 30 April 2023 count 12 days ({{twelveAmount}}) and the last {{fourteenYears}} years count 14 days ({{fourteenAmount}}). The total is {{total}}, below the cap of {{cap}}.
guide.methodBase: The base is the monthly base pay plus diuturnidades. The daily amount is that monthly amount divided by 30.
guide.methodRates: For seniority from 1 May 2023, the compensation is 14 days of base pay and diuturnidades per full year (art. 366(1) of the Código do Trabalho, as amended by Lei n.º 13/2023). Seniority before that date keeps the earlier rate: 12 days a year from 1 October 2013.
guide.methodTransitional: Older contracts keep the earlier rates for the time already worked (art. 5 of Lei n.º 69/2013). Before 1 November 2011: one month per year until 31 October 2012, then 20 days a year until 30 September 2013. From 1 November 2011 to 30 September 2013: 20 days a year until 30 September 2013. From 1 October 2013 to 30 April 2023 every contract counts 12 days a year, except that the first three years of seniority count 18 days when the contract was less than three years old on 1 October 2013. From 1 May 2023 every year counts 14 days.
guide.methodCaps: The monthly amount cannot exceed 20 times the minimum wage ({{baseCap}} with the 2026 minimum wage of {{rmmg}}), and the whole compensation cannot exceed 12 monthly amounts, at most {{totalCapRmmg}} (240 times the minimum wage). When the part up to 30 September 2013 already reaches that cap, the later periods are not added.
guide.methodFraction: An incomplete year counts proportionally: the calculator counts whole anniversaries of the start date plus the days since the last one over the days of that year. The termination date counts as a day worked.
guide.methodTax: Information only, not part of the figure: part of a termination payment can be excluded from IRS under art. 2(4) of the CIRS, up to a limit tied to your regular pay over the last 12 months and your years of seniority. The rest is taxable income. Ask the Tax Authority or an accountant for the exact limit in your case.
guide.methodBudget: The compensation is a one-off amount. Spreading it over your upcoming months, together with any unemployment benefit you are entitled to, shows how long it covers your spending.
guide.supported: Collective dismissal, extinction of the post and unsuitability of the worker on a permanent contract, and the expiry of a fixed-term contract of certain or uncertain term, with termination in 2026.
guide.unsupportedFixedTerm: Fixed-term contracts that expired before 1 May 2023 (18 days a year under the earlier text), early termination of a fixed-term contract, and expiry caused by the worker's own declaration.
guide.unsupportedJustCause: Dismissal with just cause (disciplinary), which follows different rules.
guide.unsupportedUnlawful: Unlawful dismissal, where the court sets the compensation, in general between 15 and 45 days of base pay per year of seniority.
guide.unsupportedAgreement: Termination by mutual agreement, where the amount is negotiated and there is no legal formula.
guide.unsupportedPublic: Public-sector workers, who follow different rules.
guide.sourceLaw69: Lei n.º 69/2013, of 30 August (Diário da República): new wording of art. 366 and the transitional regime of art. 5
guide.sourceLaw13: APEL guide to the Agenda do Trabalho Digno: Lei n.º 13/2023, which raised the rate of art. 366(1) to 14 days from 1 May 2023
guide.sourceCode: Código do Trabalho, consolidated text (PGDL): arts. 344, 345 and 366
guide.reviewed: Rules reviewed on 19 November 2026 against the text of Lei n.º 69/2013, published by the Assembleia da República, and the 2026 minimum wage of 920 euros (Decreto-Lei n.º 139/2025). The 14 days a year of Lei n.º 13/2023, in force from 1 May 2023, and the 12 days and cap of art. 366 come from the APEL and DGERT summaries and the consolidated Código do Trabalho, not from the Diário da República text. We apply the 14 days only to seniority from 1 May 2023, the usual reading of the transitional rule. The fixed-term rate of 24 days and its application to every contract that expires from 1 May 2023 come from the text of Lei n.º 13/2023 reproduced by PGDL (arts. 344, 345 and 35) and the IGeFE note, not from the Diário da República page. Educational, not legal advice.
guide.methodFixedTerm: Expiry of a fixed-term contract (arts. 344(2) and 345(4) of the Código do Trabalho, as amended by Lei n.º 13/2023): 24 days of base pay and diuturnidades per full year of seniority, calculated as in art. 366. The daily amount, the 20 times minimum wage cap on the monthly amount, the cap of 12 monthly amounts and the proportional fraction of a year all apply. Art. 35(1) of Lei n.º 13/2023 submits contracts signed before 1 May 2023 to the new text, and the IGeFE note of 5 July 2023 reads it as 24 days for every contract that expires from 1 May 2023. So the whole duration counts at 24 days whatever the start date, and the rates of permanent contracts (12, 14, 18 and 20 days) do not apply.
guide.sourceLaw13Text: Lei n.º 13/2023, of 3 April: new wording of arts. 344(2) and 345(4) of the Código do Trabalho and art. 35 on its application in time (PGDL reproduction of the Diário da República text)
guide.sourceIgefe: IGeFE, Nota Informativa n.º 10/2023 (5 July 2023): 24 days for every fixed-term contract that expires from 1 May 2023, whatever its signing date

guide.example: Someone earning {{gross}} a month on average (today's euros, 14 payments), with {{years}} years of contributions, retiring at {{age}}. The statutory pension is {{statutory}} a month, a global formation rate of {{rate}}. Retiring {{months}} months before the normal age deducts {{penalty}} and applies the sustainability factor, leaving {{monthly}} a month gross, or {{replacement}} of the salary. After IRS the pension is {{netPension}} a month. Against an estimated net pay of {{net}}, the gap is {{gap}} a month.
guide.methodReference: The reference remuneration is the average of your yearly pay over the whole career, revalued with consumer-price coefficients and divided by 14. The calculator works in today's euros: you enter an average real monthly salary and the result is also in today's euros.
guide.methodRate: The annual rate depends on slices of the reference remuneration in multiples of the IAS ({{ias}} in 2026): {{rates}} for the slices up to 1.1, up to 2, up to 4, up to 8 and above 8 times the IAS. Careers of up to 20 years use a flat 2%. The rate is multiplied by the years of contributions, at most 40, to give the global formation rate.
guide.methodAges: The normal age of access to the old-age pension is {{normal2026}} in 2026 and has been set at {{normal2027}} for 2027. The calculator uses the 2026 value.
guide.methodEarly: Before the normal age, from age 60 with at least 15 years of contributions, each month of anticipation takes off {{penalty}}, and the 2026 sustainability factor ({{factor}}, a 17.63% cut) also applies. The two multiply. Exemptions, such as very long careers, are not modelled.
guide.methodLate: After the normal age, up to 70, each month adds a bonus that depends on the years of contributions: 0.33% from 15 years, 0.50% from 25, 0.65% from 35 and 1% from 40. The pension with the bonus cannot exceed 92% of the reference remuneration.
guide.methodMinimum: If the formula gives less than the 2026 minimum pension for your career, the minimum is shown instead: {{min15}} for 15 to 20 years, {{min21}} for 21 to 30 and {{min31}} for 31 or more. The minimum does not apply to early retirement.
guide.methodGap: The gap compares the net pension with your net pay today, both per payment over 14 payments. Net pay is the gross salary minus 11% Social Security and the 2026 IRS withholding for a single person without dependants on the mainland. The net pension is the estimated gross pension minus IRS withheld under the 2026 pension table VIII (Despacho n.º 233-A/2026, unmarried holder or married with two earners, without disability); pensions pay no Social Security and pensions up to 920 euros a month have no withholding. The final IRS depends on your whole income and deductions.
guide.methodBudget: Read the gap as the monthly amount your savings and investments would have to cover. It moves with every assumption above.
guide.unsupportedMixed: Careers that began before 2002 (mixed formula, with the older rules for the years up to 2001). This calculator only covers the whole-career formula for people who started contributing in 2002 or later.
guide.unsupportedSpecial: Pay that varies a lot over the career, gaps in contributions and careers longer than 40 years.
guide.unsupportedCga: Civil servants in the CGA, self-employed workers and other special regimes.
guide.unsupportedOther: Early-retirement regimes without penalty, disability pensions and updates to the pension after retirement.
guide.sourceLaw: Decreto-Lei n.º 187/2007, as amended (Diário da República)

method.title: How it is calculated
method.intro: For every year in your range the calculator does the same four things:

steps.a: It adds the money invested on 1 January: your initial amount in the first year and the yearly contribution in every year.
steps.b: It grows the balance by that year's return: the total return if dividends are reinvested, the price return if not.
steps.c: If you ask for inflation-adjusted values, it divides by US consumer prices (CPI), so every figure is in the start year's dollars. Contributions are deflated with the prices of the day they are made.
steps.d: It records the value at 31 December for the table and the chart.

method.cagr: The CAGR is the geometric mean of the yearly returns in the range, in the terms you chose. It describes the index over those years and does not depend on how much you contribute.
method.contributions: Yearly contributions are added on 1 January, before that year's return, so they earn the whole year.
method.limits: The first year in the data is {{first}} and the last complete year is {{last}}. Each amount is capped at {{maxAmount}}.

data.title: Data and method
data.source: Returns are computed by WonderMoney from the year-end S&P 500 level and the dividends in Aswath Damodaran's dataset "Historical Returns on Stocks, Bonds and Bills" (NYU Stern), downloaded on {{downloaded}}. Inflation comes from the consumer price index (CPI) in Robert J. Shiller's public dataset "U.S. Stock Markets 1871-Present and CAPE Ratio" (Yale University), downloaded on {{shillerDownloaded}}.
data.method: For each calendar year the price return is the year-end level divided by the previous year-end level, minus one. The total return adds the year's dividends to the year-end level before dividing, which treats the dividends as reinvested at the year end. Inflation is the change in the CPI between the same two Decembers.
data.check: As a check, every year's total return was compared with the total return Damodaran publishes himself, and none differs by more than 0.1 percentage point. Because years run from year-end to year-end, they line up with the calendar-year figures usually quoted for the index.
data.trademark: "S&P 500" and "S&P Composite" only name the index. This page shows yearly values derived from public academic data and no daily prices, and is not affiliated with or endorsed by S&P Dow Jones Indices.

items.fx: Currency: returns are in US dollars. If you invest from the euro area, the euro-dollar exchange rate adds to or takes away from these figures, sometimes by several points a year. Currency risk is separate from the market's.
items.fees: Costs: fund fees, brokerage charges and spreads are not deducted. A fund that tracks the index returns the index minus its costs.
items.taxes: Taxes: tax on dividends and gains is not included, and it depends on where you live.
items.sequence: Hindsight: this is one large US index in one country's history. Other markets and periods did far worse, and moving the start or end by a few years can change the result a lot.
items.past: Past performance does not predict future returns. This tool is educational and is not investment advice.

read.title: How to read this page
read.estimator: The estimator prices one 30-day month on the regulated tariff: the contracted power charge, the energy you use, the audiovisual contribution and the electricity tax, then adds VAT line by line at the rate that applies to each.
read.index: The index view looks at all household bills, not just the regulated tariff: Eurostat's average price per kWh in Portugal and in the EU, taxes included, so the two are comparable.
read.market: The regulated tariff is one option. Most households are in the free market, where suppliers set their own prices and offers can be cheaper or dearer than the regulated tariff. The VAT rules are the same in both. The estimator is a reference point, not a recommendation.

example.title: Worked example
example.setup: A household with {{kva}} kVA contracted that uses {{kwh}} kWh in a month on the simple tariff. Power: {{powerPrice}} for 30 days. Energy: {{kwh}} kWh at {{energySimple}}. Plus the audiovisual contribution ({{cav}}) and the electricity tax ({{iec}}). With VAT ({{vatSimple}} in all) the month costs {{totalSimple}}, or {{effective}} once the fixed charges are spread over the kWh.
example.bi: On the bi-hourly tariff ({{energyPeak}} outside off-peak, {{energyValley}} in off-peak hours) with half the consumption in off-peak hours, the same month costs {{totalBi}}.
example.power: Contracted power matters too: at 6.9 kVA and 300 kWh the month costs {{totalBigger}}, because a higher power has a higher daily charge and its power term pays the full VAT rate.

method.title: How it is calculated
method.intro: For one 30-day month the estimator does the same five things:

steps.a: Power: the daily price for your contracted power, times 30 days.
steps.b: Energy: your kWh at the simple price, or split between the two bi-hourly prices by the share you enter.
steps.c: Audiovisual contribution (CAV): a fixed monthly amount, with reduced VAT.
steps.d: Electricity consumption tax (IEC): a fixed amount per kWh, with the standard VAT rate.
steps.e: VAT on each line, then the sum. The result is rounded to the cent at the end.

method.vat: VAT rules, as ERSE explains them: the reduced rate ({{reduced}}) applies to the first {{allowance}} kWh of energy in 30 days ({{allowanceLarge}} kWh for households of five or more) for contracted power up to 6.9 kVA, to the power term for contracted power up to 3.45 kVA, and to the audiovisual contribution. Everything else pays {{standard}}.
method.bi: Bi-hourly versus simple: the simple price is {{energySimple}}, against {{energyPeak}} outside off-peak and {{energyValley}} in off-peak hours. On energy alone the two cost the same when {{breakEven}}% of the consumption is in off-peak hours. With a lower share simple is cheaper, with a higher one bi-hourly is.
method.days: The reduced-VAT allowance is per 30 days, the period used here. A real bill for a longer or shorter period scales the allowance by its number of days.

aforro.name: Savings certificates (Certificados de Aforro)
aforro.text: Public debt issued by the Portuguese State and run by IGCP, the Treasury and public debt agency, for people with a Portuguese tax number. Série F lasts up to 15 years. Its rate follows the 3-month Euribor and adds a permanence bonus that grows the longer you hold. Interest accrues every quarter and is added to the balance after IRS. The first purchase is at least 100 units of €1 and later ones at least 10. You can redeem from the first quarterly interest date, losing the interest of the quarter in progress.

tesouro.name: Treasury certificates (Certificados do Tesouro)
tesouro.text: Also State debt run by IGCP, and still on sale in 2026: the new Série 5, open since July 2026, replaced the Poupança Valor series, which no longer takes subscriptions. At launch it paid a fixed rate rising each year, from 2.35% in year one to 3.35% in year ten, with interest paid yearly. The minimum is €1,000 and the maximum €1 million per holder. You can redeem from the end of the first year, losing the interest of the year in progress. Rates for new subscriptions can change.

demand.name: Remunerated current account
demand.text: A current account that pays interest on the balance. The money is available at any time with no loss of interest, but the rate can change and sometimes depends on conditions the bank sets. It is covered by the Deposit Guarantee Fund up to the limit.

savings.name: Savings account
savings.text: A deposit account for savings, often linked to a current account. Some accept transfers straight from another bank, others only from the linked account. Most allow withdrawals at any time, and many without losing interest. It is covered by the Deposit Guarantee Fund up to the limit.

term.name: Term deposit
term.text: You lock in an amount for a set term at a rate agreed upfront. You cannot add to it, and most pay the interest at the end of the term. Early withdrawal is allowed by only some, and usually costs half or more of the interest accrued. It is covered by the Deposit Guarantee Fund up to the limit.

capitalisation.name: Capitalisation insurance
capitalisation.text: A life insurance contract that accumulates savings. The guarantee is the insurer's, not the Deposit Guarantee Fund's, and whether capital is guaranteed depends on the contract, so check it. Most charge a fee on early withdrawal in the first years. The gain is taxed when you withdraw, and the rate falls the longer you hold.

ppr.name: PPR insurance (retirement savings plan)
ppr.text: A retirement savings plan sold here as insurance. Like capitalisation insurance, the guarantee is the insurer's and depends on the contract. Early withdrawal carries a fee in the first years unless it is for a reason set out in law, such as retirement, long-term unemployment, serious illness or permanent incapacity. Deducting contributions in your IRS return comes with conditions: see the tax section.

fgd.title: The Deposit Guarantee Fund
fgd.p1: The Fundo de Garantia de Depósitos (FGD) repays deposits at its member banks, up to €100,000 per depositor and per bank, if a bank cannot pay.
fgd.p2: It covers current, savings and term deposits. The limit is per bank: balances you hold at the same bank add up to one €100,000 limit, while balances at different banks are each covered up to their own limit.
fgd.p3: It does not cover savings or treasury certificates, which are State debt, nor insurance, which relies on the insurer. An account at a bank in another country is usually covered by that country's scheme, not the Portuguese one.

tax.title: How IRS applies
tax.intro: Interest and gains from savings are capital income (category E of IRS). The rules differ by product.

domestic.title: Certificates and Portuguese banks
domestic.text: Interest is taxed by withholding at source at 28%, a final rate (CIRS art. 71). You can choose to add it to the rest of your income instead (englobamento), in which case the amount withheld counts as a payment on account.

foreign.title: Foreign banks
foreign.text: A bank abroad does not withhold Portuguese tax. If you are resident in Portugal you must declare the interest in your IRS return, where it is taxed at 28% unless you choose englobamento (CIRS art. 72).

insurance.title: Capitalisation insurance
insurance.text: The gain is taxed when you withdraw, at 28%. If you held the contract for more than 5 and up to 8 years, a fifth of the gain is excluded (22.4%), and after 8 years three fifths are (11.2%). These reductions apply only if at least 35% of the premiums were paid in the first half of the contract (CIRS art. 5(3)).

ppr.title: PPR
ppr.text: If you withdraw for a reason set out in law, the gain is taxed at 8% (20% on two fifths of it). Outside those cases the gain is taxed at 20%, reduced to 16% after 5 years and to 8% after 8 years if at least 35% of contributions were paid in the first half. You also give back what you deducted in your IRS return, plus 10% for each year or part of a year, except after 5 years in the cases set out in law (EBF art. 21).

howToCalculateNetWorth.heroTitle: How to Calculate Your Net Worth
howToCalculateNetWorth.heroSubtitle: Net worth is the single most important number in personal finance. Here is exactly how to calculate it — and how to track it automatically.
howToCalculateNetWorth.whatBody: Net worth is the difference between everything you own (assets) and everything you owe (liabilities). It is the financial equivalent of a balance sheet — a snapshot of where you stand right now.
howToCalculateNetWorth.formulaLabel: Net Worth = Total Assets − Total Liabilities
howToCalculateNetWorth.whyTitle: Why Net Worth Matters More Than Income
howToCalculateNetWorth.whyBody: Income tells you how much flows in. Net worth tells you how much you have actually kept. Two people with the same salary can have wildly different net worths depending on their spending habits, debt levels, and investment decisions. Net worth is the scoreboard that actually matters.
howToCalculateNetWorth.assetsBody: Assets are everything you own that has financial value. Be thorough — most people underestimate their assets by forgetting certain categories.
howToCalculateNetWorth.assetCategory3Items: Market value of any property you own (not the purchase price)
howToCalculateNetWorth.assetNote: Use current market value, not purchase price or sentimental value. Your pension pot counts — check your most recent statement.
howToCalculateNetWorth.liabilitiesBody: Liabilities are everything you owe. Include the outstanding balance, not the original loan amount.
howToCalculateNetWorth.liabilityCategory1Items: Outstanding balance on any property loan
howToCalculateNetWorth.liabilityCategory2Items: Car loans, personal loans, credit card balances
howToCalculateNetWorth.liabilityCategory4Items: BNPL balances, money owed to friends or family
howToCalculateNetWorth.calculateTitle: Step 3: Subtract to Get Your Number
howToCalculateNetWorth.calculateBody: Once you have both totals, the calculation is straightforward: subtract total liabilities from total assets. The result is your net worth. It can be positive or negative — negative is common early in life when mortgage and student loan balances dominate.
howToCalculateNetWorth.trackBody: A one-time calculation is useful. Monthly tracking is transformative. Watching your net worth grow month by month makes the impact of your saving and investment decisions visible. It also reveals problems early — months where net worth shrinks despite stable income are a signal worth investigating.
howToCalculateNetWorth.autoBody: Doing this manually every month requires pulling data from every bank, broker, and loan account. WonderMoney connects directly to your bank accounts via Open Banking and imports your investment portfolio, then calculates and updates your net worth every day automatically — no spreadsheet required.
howToCalculateNetWorth.faq1Q: Should I include my pension in net worth?
howToCalculateNetWorth.faq1A: Yes. Your pension pot is an asset. Include the current value from your most recent pension statement. It is illiquid, but it is real wealth.
howToCalculateNetWorth.faq2Q: Should I include my home in net worth?
howToCalculateNetWorth.faq2A: Include your home at current market value (not purchase price), then subtract the outstanding mortgage as a liability. The difference — your equity — is part of your net worth.
howToCalculateNetWorth.faq3Q: How often should I calculate my net worth?
howToCalculateNetWorth.faq3A: Monthly is ideal. It is frequent enough to spot trends and react to changes, but not so frequent that short-term market fluctuations cause unnecessary anxiety.
howToCalculateNetWorth.faq4Q: What is a good net worth by age?
howToCalculateNetWorth.faq4A: There is no universal answer — it depends on income, country, family situation, and goals. A useful benchmark: aim for net worth equal to 1x your annual income by age 30, 3x by 40, and 6x by 50.

openBankingApp.faq2A: No. Open Banking connections in WonderMoney are strictly read-only. WonderMoney can see your balance and transactions, but it can never initiate a payment or move money.
openBankingApp.faq3Q: Who is WonderMoney's Open Banking provider?
openBankingApp.faq3A: WonderMoney uses Enable Banking, a Registered Account Information Service Provider regulated by Finland's Financial Supervisory Authority (FIN-FSA) and one of Europe's established Open Banking infrastructure providers.
openBankingApp.faq4Q: What happens if I disconnect my bank?
openBankingApp.faq4A: You can revoke access at any time, from WonderMoney or directly from your bank's app. Historical data already synced stays in your account unless you delete it.
openBankingApp.ctaHeadline: Connect Your Bank Accounts the Secure Way
openBankingApp.ctaBody: Link your accounts via Open Banking and let WonderMoney keep your financial picture up to date automatically. Free and open source.

budgetApp.metaDescription: WonderMoney is a budget app that connects to your European bank accounts via Open Banking, automatically categorises transactions, and helps you budget by category — solo or with a partner.
budgetApp.feature1Body: Set a monthly budget for rent, groceries, transport, and more. WonderMoney matches incoming transactions to the right category automatically.
budgetApp.feature2Body: Your bank transactions sync daily via Open Banking. WonderMoney categorises them automatically and deducts from the right budget.
budgetApp.feature3Body: Every category shows how much you've spent and how much is left, so overspending shows up before the month is over, not after.
budgetApp.feature4Body: Compare what you planned to spend against what you actually spent, category by category, and adjust next month accordingly.
budgetApp.feature5Body: Multi-currency support (EUR, GBP, USD and 8 more), so budgets work whether your accounts are in one currency or several.
budgetApp.feature6Body: Household mode lets two people share budgets and categories, so couples can plan spending together instead of guessing.
budgetApp.how1Body: Create budget categories for the things you spend on — rent, groceries, transport, subscriptions — and set a monthly amount for each.
budgetApp.how2Body: Link your accounts via Open Banking. Transactions sync automatically and match to the right budget category.
budgetApp.how3Title: Review and adjust as you go
budgetApp.how3Body: Check your budgets anytime to see what's on track and what's overspent, and move money between categories when plans change.
budgetApp.faq1Q: Do I have to enter transactions manually?
budgetApp.faq1A: No. WonderMoney connects to your bank via Open Banking and imports transactions automatically, matching each one to a budget category.
budgetApp.faq2Q: What budgeting method does WonderMoney use?
budgetApp.faq2A: WonderMoney supports category-based budgeting: you allocate a monthly amount to each category, and spending is tracked against it automatically as transactions arrive.
budgetApp.faq3Q: Can I budget with my partner?
budgetApp.faq3A: Yes. Household mode lets two people share budgets, categories, and accounts in one place, with billing managed by a single plan.
budgetApp.faq4A: Yes. WonderMoney is free to use at wonder.money, or you can run it on your own server.
budgetApp.ctaHeadline: Start Budgeting Without the Manual Work
budgetApp.ctaBody: Connect your bank accounts and let WonderMoney track your budget automatically. Free and open source.

adNetWorth.metaTitle: Do You Know What You're Worth? — WonderMoney
adNetWorth.metaDescription: See your complete net worth in one place — bank accounts, investments, and debts combined automatically. Free and open source.
adNetWorth.heroTitle: Do you actually know what you're worth?
adNetWorth.heroSubtitle: Most people can tell you their salary to the euro. Almost nobody can tell you their real net worth. WonderMoney connects your accounts and investments to show you the number that actually matters.
adNetWorth.painTitle: Why most people have no idea
adNetWorth.pain1Body: A current account here, a savings account there, an investment platform somewhere else. Nobody adds it all up — so nobody knows the real total.
adNetWorth.pain2Body: Even if you built a net worth spreadsheet once, updating it by hand every month is the first habit to slip.
adNetWorth.pain3Body: Net worth isn't just what you own — it's what you own minus what you owe. Most people only track one side of that equation.
adNetWorth.how1Body: Link your bank accounts and investment platforms via secure, read-only Open Banking.
adNetWorth.how2Body: Balances, portfolio value, and debts combine into one net worth figure that updates as your providers supply new data.
adNetWorth.how3Body: See your net worth trend month by month, so you know if you're actually moving in the right direction.
adNetWorth.ctaHeadline: Find out what you're actually worth
adNetWorth.ctaBody: Connect your accounts and see your real net worth — automatically, in one place.

adFragmentation.heroTitle: 5 bank apps. 2 broker apps. 1 spreadsheet. There's a better way.
adFragmentation.heroSubtitle: You shouldn't need six logins to answer one question: how am I doing financially? WonderMoney brings every account into a single view.
adFragmentation.painTitle: Juggling apps costs you more than time
adFragmentation.pain1Title: You check five apps and still don't know the answer
adFragmentation.pain1Body: Each app shows one slice of your finances. None of them shows the whole picture — so the real question stays unanswered.
adFragmentation.pain2Title: The spreadsheet is always out of date
adFragmentation.pain2Body: You built it once to tie everything together. Updating it by hand every month is the part that never survives.
adFragmentation.pain3Body: When your accounts live in five different places, it's easy for a subscription or fee to slip past you unseen.
adFragmentation.how1Body: Link your bank accounts and investment platforms via secure, read-only Open Banking — no more switching apps.
adFragmentation.how2Body: Balances, spending, and investments sit side by side, automatically categorized and kept in sync.
adFragmentation.how3Body: Open WonderMoney and get the full picture — no more app-hopping to piece it together.
adFragmentation.ctaBody: Connect every account and see your whole financial picture in a single place.

adOpenBanking.metaTitle: Your Bank Has to Share Your Data If You Ask — WonderMoney
adOpenBanking.metaDescription: EU law requires your bank to share your data with apps you authorize. WonderMoney uses this to show your full financial picture automatically. Free and open source.
adOpenBanking.heroTitle: Your bank is legally required to share your data with apps you authorize. Most people don't know this.
adOpenBanking.heroSubtitle: Open Banking (PSD2) gives you the right to connect your accounts to apps like WonderMoney — securely, and only with your permission. It turns five separate logins into one clear picture.
adOpenBanking.painTitle: The right most people never use
adOpenBanking.pain1Title: It's not a workaround — it's the law
adOpenBanking.pain1Body: Under PSD2, EU banks must let you share your account data with authorized apps, on your terms.
adOpenBanking.pain2Title: Your bank still holds your money
adOpenBanking.pain2Body: Open Banking is read-only. WonderMoney can see your data to show it to you — it can't move money or make payments.
adOpenBanking.pain3Body: You choose which accounts to connect, and you can disconnect at any time from your bank or from WonderMoney.
adOpenBanking.how1Body: Pick your bank and confirm the connection directly with them — WonderMoney never sees your banking credentials.
adOpenBanking.how2Body: Your bank shares balances and transactions with WonderMoney under the permission you granted. Nothing more.
adOpenBanking.how3Title: See it all in one place
adOpenBanking.how3Body: Every connected account feeds into a single dashboard — balances, spending, and net worth, kept in sync.
adOpenBanking.ctaHeadline: Put your legal right to work
adOpenBanking.ctaBody: Connect your accounts and see your full financial picture — securely, on your terms.
